items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 17, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: I wasn’t very pleased that they cut out my piano solo... I was there slightly to the left of Parker

ctx.x: Yeah. I remember reading an annoying article once and the writer was basically saying that Charlie Parker would not have been able to play what he did if he hadn’t been on heroin.

I don’t know the answer to that. I just don’t know. I do know that there are on records certain magical moments in various people’s solos where you can only say to yourself where did that come from? You find it on early Armstrong, you find it on Bird’s things. But not everything that Bird did. A good deal of what Bird played was enough of a rote so that players ever since have been able to sound very much like him because he did repeat his riffs. Every now and then. I’ve heard it also in some of Beiderbecke’s…
Right. You started to mention a couple of people and I had a couple of names I was just going to throw at you, for maybe a short comment. Milt Hinton.

items.title: Dick Hyman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I remember that Bird came and sat in with us at Tony Scott’s combo... when I, the couple of times I played with him

ctx.x: I’d like to maybe turn back the clock a little bit again. I’m interested in your playing with people like Dizzy and Charlie Parker and the 52nd Street scene. Is this something you can describe to us — what that was like back then?

Well you know that famous film of Charlie Parker that I’m on just happened. I was playing a New York local daily television show with a bass player and we would accompany any singers that came on to the show. And one day it appeared that Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie would be awarded an Esquire Magazine award by Leonard Feather.
